title: Financial Services: Fears banks to follow NAB's jobs layoff lead
full_text:
National Australia Bank is slashing 2500 jobs in a move it says is aimed at becoming more efficient and responding to a tougher economy, amid fears other banks could also swing the axe to boost profitability.
The banking giant made the announcement yesterday, saying up to 1500 jobs would go before the end of the 2026 calendar year. It will also reduce its use of consultants and external contractors.
NAB chief executive Andrew Irvine said the moves were designed to make the bank more efficient and that the cuts would have no "material impact to customer-facing roles".
"We will improve productivity, risk outcomes and execution to be a simpler and more efficient bank. These changes are expected to improve outcomes for customers by reducing duplication and speeding up decision-making. We are particularly focused on reducing the size of corporate functions," Irvine said.
"We know this will be a difficult period for our colleagues impacted by these changes as well as the people around them. We will treat every person with dignity and respect."
The Finance Sector Union said it was appalled by the cuts, which it said "will wreak chaos and entrench a culture of anxiety at a bank that seems hell-bent on self-destruction".
"To take a wrecking ball to 6 per cent of one of Australia's largest workforces this close to Christmas is disgraceful and shows that NAB's leadership is completely detached from the lived experience of their workers," the union's national assistant secretary, Nicole McPherson, said.
"NAB's public statement today is full of nothing put corporate spin and confirms the bank is in denial about the significant impact these cuts will have on a workforce already overwhelmed by unmanageable workloads."
At a press conference held in the hours after union officials met with NAB leadership, McPherson said she was concerned other banks would follow suit with job cuts.
"When they make billions and billions of dollars a year, we're seeing that even though they could absolutely afford to have a quality workforce in Australia, they're choosing not to because they're choosing to pad their already massive profits at the expense of Australian workers," McPherson said.
The cuts mimic a significant cull by ANZ, which last year announced it was slashing costs by sacking 3500 employees and another 1000 contractors but also emphasised that the cuts would not be at the expense of customer-facing roles.
ANZ's cull, which finished last month, was described by new ANZ chief executive Nuno Matos as a very difficult but necessary step to simplify its operations and shore up the bank's long-term viability.
Like Matos, Irvine plans to use the savings made to shore up the bank's defences amid intensifying competition, and to invest in priority growth areas.
Business growth areas he highlighted yesterday included growing its market-leading business banking division, increasing customer deposits and strengthening its home lending rather than relying on external brokers to generate business.
An NAB spokeswoman would not specify which teams or divisions the cuts would come from. The spokeswoman also reiterated the cuts were about simplifying the bank's operating model, and said that while artificial intelligence will continue to change how work is done across the bank, the cuts don't reflect widespread replacement of roles by AI.
NAB's shares slumped on the news but recovered slightly to close at $39.20.
Analysts from investment bank Jarden called NAB's push to transform its business "belated" and said the bank lags rival ANZ by about two years.
"There is no real detail yet on how this will increase growth and enhance technology initiatives for customers apart from reducing duplication, shrinking the corporate centre (bureaucracy) and streamlining decision-making, which should ordinarily be part of running the business," they wrote in a note to clients.
NAB's move comes amid a broader disruption the entire banking industry is facing from IT advancement, the analysts explained.
NAB said the cuts were expected to generate restructuring costs of about $300 million pre-tax for the 2027 financial year, which started on October 1.
It said further details on the cost outlook for the financial year will be provided with the release of its 2026 financial results on November 5.
